modules.title: Health and wellbeing
modules.summary: Distinguish arranged services with causative verbs (have/get something done) and present public health findings neutrally with passive reporting.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Wellbeing, preventive care and daily habits

grammar.name: Causative verbs
grammar.explanation: Use have or get something done when someone else performs a service for you, and have someone do something when you arrange it directly.
keyPoints: Service: I had my blood pressure checked last week.
Arrangement: She got the pharmacy to deliver the prescription.
Trouble: He had his appendix removed on Monday.
grammar.example: I had my eyes tested on Friday and got the optician to adjust the lenses for free.

items.prompt: I ___ my blood pressure checked last week.
items.explanation: Have + object + past participle shows a service performed by someone else.

items.prompt: Which sentence means someone else did the work?
items.explanation: The causative makes the agent of the action someone other than the subject.

items.prompt: She ___ the pharmacy to deliver the prescription.
items.explanation: Get + person + to + infinitive describes persuading or arranging.

grammar.name: Passive reporting
grammar.explanation: Report widely held beliefs or medical findings formally with "It is believed/estimated that…" or "Subject + is thought to + infinitive".
keyPoints: Impersonal frame: It is widely recognised that poor sleep affects concentration.
Personal frame: Short afternoon walks are thought to reduce stress levels.
Use "to have + past participle" for an earlier event: Stress is thought to have contributed to the rise.
grammar.example: Regular walking is widely reported to lower blood pressure, so more patients are getting their check-ups booked early.

items.prompt: Adequate sleep ___ to improve memory consolidation overnight.
items.explanation: Passive reporting uses "is known/thought/believed + to-infinitive".

items.prompt: It is ___ estimated that sitting all day raises discomfort in the lower back.
items.explanation: Collocation: "widely estimated / reported / recognised".

items.prompt: Older residents ___ their prescriptions delivered directly by a local pharmacist.
items.explanation: Causative "have + object + past participle" describes an arranged service.

inputs.title: Panel discussion: whose responsibility is health?
inputs.body: CHAIR: Whose responsibility is health? DR OSEI: I get uncomfortable when we talk only about individual choice, because choice is shaped. If the only shop within a kilometre sells processed food, that is not a free choice. DR LEWIS: I agree up to a point, but people do respond to information. Smoking fell for decades before any ban, largely because attitudes changed. CHAIR: So is taxation part of the answer? DR OSEI: It can be, provided the revenue goes back into prevention. Otherwise it just looks like a fine on being poor. Later in the programme, the physiotherapist explained why small workplace adjustments matter just as much as weekend exercise. Many desk workers never get their chair height or screen distance checked until neck pain sets in. It is increasingly recognised that short five-minute movement breaks every hour protect focus as well as posture. Meanwhile, the community nutritionist noted that people cut down on ultra-processed snacks much more easily when healthy lunches are affordable near schools and train stations.

questions.prompt: Why does Dr Osei distrust the 'individual choice' argument?
options: Because choice is shaped by the environment
questions.answer: Because choice is shaped by the environment

questions.prompt: What condition does Dr Osei set for taxation?
options: It must apply only to the rich

inputs.title: Should junk food be taxed? Two views
inputs.body: FOR: The case is straightforward. Sugar taxes reduce consumption, and consumption of sugar raises the risk of diseases that cost public health systems billions. A levy of ten per cent in one European country cut purchases of sugary drinks by eighteen per cent within a year, and the revenue funded free school meals. AGAINST: The case is equally straightforward. Such taxes are regressive: they take a larger share of income from poorer households, who also have less time to cook and fewer affordable alternatives. Education and better labelling would achieve more, and would not punish people for buying what is cheapest. Public health researchers also point out that labelling rules and local environment play a decisive role. When supermarkets place sugary drinks at eye level near every checkout, busy parents face constant nudges, whereas clear nutritional labelling makes healthier swaps straightforward. At the same time, critics warn that taxes alone rarely change habits unless revenue helps fund sports clubs, cycling routes, and affordable fresh produce in lower-income neighbourhoods. Ultimately, combining clear public information with practical neighbourhood support is widely thought to deliver steadier improvements than blame or strict bans. Employers and schools are also discovering that small structural nudges outperform dramatic wellness posters. Offering flexible walking meetings, keeping quiet break rooms free from work screens, and subsidising seasonal fruit bowls cost relatively little compared with high staff turnover. Even simple sleep hygiene workshops—encouraging people to dim bright screens an hour before bed and keep steady waking times—often improve afternoon focus more reliably than extra coffee. When healthier options become the easiest default on an ordinary Tuesday, citizens do not have to rely purely on willpower to protect long-term physical and mental wellbeing.

options: An eighteen per cent drop in purchases
questions.answer: An eighteen per cent drop in purchases

writing.title: Argument essay: health and responsibility
writing.prompt: Write a 180–200 word argument essay: should governments tax unhealthy products to improve public health? Present both sides and reach a clear conclusion.

outline.analyze: Purpose: argue and conclude. Audience: an examiner or opinion page. Register: formal.
outline.plan: Introduction with position → argument for → argument against → evaluation → conclusion.
outline.draft: Use at least three advanced linkers and one causative structure.
outline.improve: Qualify your claims; replace absolutes with hedging where evidence is limited.
outline.review: Check that the conclusion follows from the evaluation, not from repetition.

modules.title: Cities, transport and society
modules.summary: Consolidate article and quantifier precision for abstract urban issues, and weigh policies accurately using varied comparative structures.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Urban planning, transit and liveable neighbourhoods

grammar.name: Articles and quantifiers (consolidation)
grammar.explanation: Combine zero article for general uncountable concepts (traffic, pollution, housing) with "the" for specific urban policies and precise quantifiers (a great deal of, far fewer, hardly any).
keyPoints: Use "the + singular countable" only for specific institutions or generic inventions (the underground, the bicycle).
Use far fewer / several with plural countables and far less / a considerable amount of with uncountables.
Remember that housing, transport, research, and congestion are uncountable.
grammar.example: Cities with reliable trams see far fewer traffic jams and spend a great deal less on road repairs.

items.prompt: Pedestrian zones produce ___ noise than multi-lane ring roads.
items.explanation: Noise is uncountable, so compare with "much less".

items.prompt: ___ affordable housing remains one of the sharpest challenges in capital cities.
items.explanation: General uncountable noun phrases ("affordable housing") take zero article.

items.prompt: Only ___ residents objected once the cycle lane opened safely.
items.explanation: "Residents" is plural countable, so use "a few".

grammar.name: Comparative structures
grammar.explanation: Move past basic -er/more with B2 modifiers (far more, marginally quieter, nowhere near as expensive as) and double comparatives (the more…, the less…).
keyPoints: Gradable modifiers: considerably faster, slightly cheaper, nowhere near as reliable as.
Double comparatives show cause-and-effect: The more frequent the trains, the fewer cars enter the centre.
Use "as… as" to compare equality or shortfall cleanly.
grammar.example: The more reliable regional rail becomes, the less tempting it is to drive—and electric buses are nowhere near as noisy as older diesel fleets.

items.prompt: The wider the pavements are, ___ pleasant the high street feels.
items.explanation: Double comparative structure: "The + comparative..., the + comparative...".

items.prompt: Regional buses are ___ as punctual as express trains during rush hour.
items.explanation: "Nowhere near as + adjective + as" emphasises a big gap.

items.prompt: Walking is ___ healthier and cheaper than sitting in traffic.
items.explanation: "Considerably" modifies an existing comparative ("healthier"); avoid "much more healthier".

inputs.title: The fifteen-minute neighbourhood: reality or slogan?
inputs.body: Hannah: Almost every mayor talks about liveable cities now, yet commuters still spend hours stuck in traffic. Tariq, you study urban transport across mid-sized European and Canadian towns. Why do some neighbourhoods feel effortless to walk around while others feel exhausting? Tariq: Honestly, it comes down to two practical details: safe street crossings and mixed-use zoning. When a district has only office towers or only rows of houses, people have no choice except to drive or crowd onto trains during peak hours. By contrast, where bakeries, primary schools, clinics, and parks sit within a fifteen-minute walk, far fewer short car journeys are needed. Hannah: Critics sometimes complain that pedestrianising centres hurts small shops or pushes rents higher. Is there truth in that? Tariq: There can be if councils stop at cosmetic paving. The cities that succeed pair car-free streets with strict affordable housing quotas and fast step-free buses linking outer estates to the centre. The better outer districts are connected, the less pressure builds up on historic streets. Good transit is nowhere near as expensive as widening motorways—and it leaves far more room for trees and benches.

questions.prompt: According to Tariq, what two details make a neighbourhood easy to walk around?
options: Larger car parks and wider motorways
Safe street crossings and mixed-use zoning
Taller office towers and night buses
questions.answer: Safe street crossings and mixed-use zoning

questions.prompt: How do successful cities prevent pedestrianisation from hurting outer residents?
options: By pairing car-free zones with affordable housing quotas and fast buses
By closing all outer bus routes
By charging pedestrians to enter parks
questions.answer: By pairing car-free zones with affordable housing quotas and fast buses

inputs.title: What makes a city street feel genuinely alive?
inputs.body: Walk through two neighbourhoods with similar population density and you may experience completely different atmospheres. On one street, pavements are narrow, blank walls line the ground floor, and delivery vans idle beside fast-moving traffic; pedestrians hurry past without looking up. Three blocks away, wider pavements, street trees, small independent grocers, and benches invite neighbours to pause and chat. Urban planners argue that liveability has far less to do with shiny skyscrapers than with what happens at eye level. When ground floors hold bookshops, repair cafés, clinics, and libraries rather than shuttered garages, streets feel considerably safer after dusk because ordinary people are naturally around. Transport infrastructure shapes that social life just as strongly. Cities that prioritise step-free accessibility, shaded bus shelters, and protected cycle lanes allow children, commuters, and older residents to share space comfortably without relying on private cars for every short errand. Of course, attractive districts can trigger rising rents and rapid gentrification if local authorities ignore housing supply. Protecting long-standing workshops and funding affordable housing alongside cleaner transit ensures that revitalised streets serve the whole community rather than pricing residents out. Encouragingly, several European and Latin American towns have proved that fairer street design does not require decades of underground tunnelling. Painted bus-priority lanes, secure cycle hangars on residential corners, and frequent weekend regional trains can transform daily mobility within two or three budget cycles. Residents who previously drove short three-kilometre errands willingly switch when walking routes feel well-lit, continuous, and pleasant in poor weather. Meanwhile, preserving ground-floor leases for independent pharmacies, repair workshops, and grocers keeps essential errands local, reducing congestion across the whole city while protecting social connection for older neighbours.

questions.prompt: Why do planners focus on what happens at eye level on a street?
options: Tall skyscrapers are illegal in historic centres
Active ground-floor shops and spaces encourage safety and social contact
questions.answer: Active ground-floor shops and spaces encourage safety and social contact

questions.prompt: What risk does the essay warn about when a neighbourhood becomes more attractive?
options: Rising rents and gentrification unless affordable housing is protected
Too many public libraries opening at night
questions.answer: Rising rents and gentrification unless affordable housing is protected

modules.title: Art, culture and creativity
modules.summary: Pack descriptive and analytical prose smoothly using participle clauses and reduced relative clauses.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Museums, cinema, creative work and funding

grammar.name: Participle clauses
grammar.explanation: Use present (-ing), past (-ed), or perfect (having + past participle) clauses to link time, reason, or background concisely—making sure both clauses share the same subject.
keyPoints: Having visited the exhibition twice, she noticed subtle brushwork she had missed first time.
Built in 1894, the theatre still hosts community plays every autumn.
Avoid dangling participles: the subject after the comma must be the person/thing doing the participle action.
grammar.example: Inspired by local folk tales, the director spent three winters filming along the coast.

items.prompt: ___ in 1928, the cinema recently reopened as an independent arts centre.
items.explanation: Passive meaning ("which was built") uses the past participle "Built".

items.prompt: ___ read the director’s notes, I understood the ending much better.
items.explanation: "Having + past participle" shows one action finished before the main clause.

items.prompt: Which sentence avoids a dangling participle?
options: Walking into the gallery, the sculptures immediately impressed us.
Walking into the gallery, we were immediately impressed by the sculptures.
Walking into the gallery, a large crowd was blocking the entrance.
items.answer: Walking into the gallery, we were immediately impressed by the sculptures.
items.explanation: "We" are the ones walking into the gallery, matching the participle clause subject.

grammar.name: Reduced relative clauses
grammar.explanation: Shorten defining relative clauses cleanly by dropping "who/which/that + be" before active -ing or passive -ed phrases.
keyPoints: Active: Visitors hoping to catch the evening talk (= who hope) should arrive early.
Passive: Photographs taken during the rehearsal (= which were taken) are displayed upstairs.
Never reduce a relative clause when the relative pronoun is the object of the verb.
grammar.example: Artists applying for the residency (= who are applying) must submit work completed within the past two years.

items.prompt: The mural ___ by neighbourhood teenagers brightens the whole underpass.
items.explanation: Passive reduced relative clause ("which was painted").

items.prompt: Musicians ___ in small venues often rely on ticket sales rather than streaming.
items.explanation: Active reduced relative clause ("who perform").

items.prompt: Anyone ___ to attend Friday’s play should collect a pass at reception.
items.explanation: "Anyone wishing" replaces "anyone who wishes".

inputs.title: Why regional arts venues matter
inputs.body: Claire: When municipal budgets get tight, cultural grants are often the first line cut. Yet artists working outside capital cities say small theatres and neighbourhood galleries are where new voices actually begin. Ben, you directed a regional arts festival in Adelaide before moving to Sheffield. What disappears when a local venue closes? Ben: Far more than a Saturday night out. Having toured towns across two continents, I have seen how a single community cinema or rehearsal studio anchors an entire high street. Young writers experimenting with their first play rarely start on a West End stage; they test ideas in rooms seating eighty people, supported by curators willing to take a risk on originality. Built inside former warehouses or Victorian town halls, these spaces also bring generations together. A photography show curated by retired dockworkers alongside school students sparks conversations you never get in mainstream multiplexes. Claire: So public patronage is really seed funding for future culture? Ben: Exactly. Making culture accessible locally gives people confidence to create, not just consume.

questions.prompt: Why does Ben say small regional venues are vital for new artists?
options: They pay higher salaries than national television
They give emerging creators space to test original work before smaller audiences
questions.answer: They give emerging creators space to test original work before smaller audiences

questions.prompt: What social benefit does Ben mention about local cultural spaces?
options: They bring different generations together around shared exhibitions
They replace local schools and colleges
They keep ticket prices above commercial theatres
questions.answer: They bring different generations together around shared exhibitions

inputs.title: Does creative boredom still have a place?
inputs.body: Ask novelists, composers, or designers where their strongest ideas first surfaced, and very few mention scrolling through a feed of trending clips. Surrounded by constant notifications and polished templates, modern creators can easily confuse rapid consumption with genuine originality. Several psychologists studying creative breakthroughs point out that the brain needs quiet, unstructured intervals to connect distant memories into something unexpected. Walking without headphones, sketching in a pocket notebook, or staring out of a train window may look unproductive on paper, yet those unhurried pauses often allow half-formed thoughts to settle. Museums and galleries curated with restraint understand this rhythm too. Exhibitions crowding fifty screens into a single room often leave visitors exhausted, whereas quieter galleries displaying twenty evocative paintings with space to sit invite sharper attention. Having stepped away from constant noise, viewers notice details—a shift in light, an unusual material, an unfinished line—that rushed viewing hides. Protecting creative space does not mean rejecting technology; rather, it means keeping room for stillness, curiosity, and slow experimentation alongside digital tools. Public arts education plays a quiet, vital role in keeping that curiosity alive across generations. When secondary schools protect time for theatre workshops, choral music, ceramics, and film editing alongside STEM subjects, teenagers discover practical ways to express complex ideas without relying purely on multiple-choice answers. Community funding also helps keep museum admissions affordable so families never feel excluded by ticket costs on wet Sunday afternoons. Whether through a small local bookshop hosting debut poets or a municipal gallery lending prints to clinics, accessible culture enriches everyday civic life far beyond major tourist festivals.

questions.prompt: What do psychologists say unstructured quiet intervals help the brain do?
options: Connect distant memories and ideas into original insights
questions.answer: Connect distant memories and ideas into original insights

questions.prompt: Why does the essay prefer restrained exhibitions over screen-crowded rooms?
options: Quiet rooms with seating invite closer attention to detail
Paintings are cheaper to insure than screens
Visitors prefer spending less than ten minutes in museums
questions.answer: Quiet rooms with seating invite closer attention to detail

modules.title: Ethics, fairness and choices
modules.summary: Add rhetorical weight to ethical arguments using negative inversion (Not only…, Seldom…) and cleft sentences for sharp focus.

grammar.name: Inversion and emphasis
grammar.explanation: After a negative or limiting adverbial at the start of a sentence, invert the subject and auxiliary to add emphasis.
keyPoints: Not only did the policy cut emissions, but it also created jobs.
Rarely have I seen such a weak argument.
Never before has the city faced this choice. / Little did we know…
grammar.example: Not only did the levy reduce consumption, but it also funded school meals; rarely has a policy faced such organised opposition.

items.prompt: Not only ___ the policy cut emissions, but it also created jobs.
items.explanation: Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb: Not only did the policy cut emissions…

items.prompt: Rarely ___ such a weak argument.
items.explanation: A fronted negative adverbial triggers inversion: Rarely have I heard…

items.prompt: Which sentence is correctly inverted?
options: Never the city has faced this choice.
Never has the city faced this choice.
Never has faced the city this choice.
items.answer: Never has the city faced this choice.
items.explanation: Auxiliary before subject, then the main verb.

grammar.name: Cleft sentences
grammar.explanation: Highlight the key reason, person, or detail in a debate using "It is… that…" or "What matters most is…".
keyPoints: It-cleft: It is clear labelling—not vague promises—that builds shopper trust.
What-cleft: What consumers actually need is transparent supply-chain data.
Use cleft sentences selectively so your emphasis stays punchy.
grammar.example: Not only did the audit expose overtime abuses, but what shocked shoppers most was how easy fixes were.

items.prompt: ___ matters most in fair-trade schemes is whether farmers receive stable prices.
items.explanation: What-cleft ("What matters most is...") puts focus on the clause after "is".

items.prompt: It was the lack of independent checks ___ undermined public trust.
items.explanation: It-cleft uses "It is/was + focus + that/who...".

items.prompt: Only when companies publish audit results ___ trust the label.
items.explanation: "Only when..." at the start triggers subject-auxiliary inversion in the main clause.

vocab.definition: the duty to accept responsibility and explain decisions openly
vocab.example: Public funding should always come with clear financial accountability.

vocab.definition: open and honest about rules, prices, or decisions so nothing is hidden
vocab.example: Transparent pricing stops hidden fees appearing on the final screen.

vocab.definition: a difficult situation where you must choose between two competing options
vocab.example: Whistleblowers often face a moral dilemma between loyalty and honesty.

vocab.definition: a rule or principle applied unfairly more strictly to one group than another
vocab.example: Employees quickly notice a double standard if senior staff ignore office rules.

vocab.definition: treat someone unfairly for your own financial or personal gain
vocab.example: Strict labour inspections help ensure seasonal workers are not exploited.

vocab.definition: the quality of being honest and sticking to strong moral principles
vocab.example: Maintaining academic integrity means citing every source accurately.

vocab.definition: a situation where private gain could improperly influence an official decision
vocab.example: Panel members must declare any conflict of interest before scoring bids.

vocab.definition: a gap in a rule or law that allows people to avoid its intended purpose
vocab.example: Lawmakers closed the tax loophole after journalists published leaked records.

vocab.definition: defend or support a person or principle openly when it is difficult
vocab.example: Colleagues respected her for standing up for junior staff during pay talks.

inputs.title: Panel debate: should cities ban cars from the centre?
inputs.body: HOST: Is a car-free centre realistic? COUNCILLOR REID: Not only has it worked elsewhere, but it has also increased footfall in the shops. That is the part people miss. TRADER MS KOVAC: With respect, that has not been our experience. Our deliveries arrive before seven, and the loading bay is gone. COUNCILLOR REID: Then let us concede that point and solve it — timed access. MS KOVAC: I would accept timed access, provided it is enforced. My worry is that it looks good in a report and fails in the street. Later in the debate, the consumer advocate raised an ethical dilemma: what happens when green policies hit lower-income households harder than wealthy drivers? Not only must councils offer fair exemptions for shift workers and disabled residents, she argued, but what builds lasting fairness is transparent communication about where congestion fees go. When every pound raised funds cleaner regional buses, citizens see tangible accountability rather than a double standard.

questions.prompt: What does Councillor Reid claim about shops?
What does Ms Kovac accept in the end?

inputs.title: Why small everyday fairness builds lasting trust
inputs.body: When people think about ethics, dramatic courtroom trials or corporate scandals usually come to mind first. Yet in ordinary workplaces, schools, and local councils, trust rises or falls on much quieter decisions: whether rules apply equally to senior leaders, whether a conflict of interest is declared before a contract is awarded, and whether someone admits a mistake without shifting blame onto junior staff. Rarely do institutions collapse overnight; instead, credibility erodes slowly whenever double standards become routine. What distinguishes healthy organisations is not perfection, since human judgement is always fallible, but visible accountability when loopholes appear. Suppose a team notices that flexible working is praised in recruitment adverts yet quietly penalised during promotion reviews. Not only does morale fall, but talented staff stop speaking honestly in meetings. Conversely, when leaders publish clear criteria, explain trade-offs transparently, and protect colleagues who stand up for fair treatment, people feel safe raising concerns early. Integrity at scale begins with small, consistent choices long before any crisis arrives. Training programmes in medicine, law, and engineering now spend far more time on realistic case studies than abstract moral puzzles. Instead of debating unlikely emergencies, trainees examine everyday pressures: what to do when a manager asks you to omit an inconvenient delay from a client summary, or how to respond when an algorithm scores applicants unevenly. Practising clear, respectful phrases for raising concerns early makes ethical courage far easier when real pressure hits. Organisations that reward honesty during routine reviews build cultures where integrity becomes normal practice rather than a risky exception.

questions.prompt: According to the essay, how does institutional credibility usually erode?
options: In a single dramatic courtroom trial
Gradually when double standards become routine
Whenever junior staff speak in meetings
questions.answer: Gradually when double standards become routine

questions.prompt: What does the essay say builds psychological safety in healthy organisations?
options: Transparent criteria, accountability, and protecting people who raise concerns
questions.answer: Transparent criteria, accountability, and protecting people who raise concerns
